name: PCR Cycle Calculator
seoDesc: A PCR run is a few dozen repeats of three steps, and the total time on the machine is simply the sum of those steps plus the ramp between them. Free pcr cycle
summary:
A PCR run is a few dozen repeats of three steps, and the total time on the machine is simply the sum of those steps plus the ramp between them. It returns time per cycle, total run time, fold amplification and copies at the end, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator turns your protocol into the time per cycle, the time to the answer and the number of copies produced. Press Calculate and the results appear in the grey boxes; after the first press they keep up with every edit, so there is no page to reload. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the PCR Cycle
sections.html:
Time per cycle = t_denature + t_anneal + t_extend + 3 × ramp; copies = N₀ × (1 + E)^cycles

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
Eefficiency per cycle (1.0 = perfect doubling)—
N₀template copies at the startcopies
ttime for each steps

sections.title: How do I use the PCR Cycle?
sections.html:
Every input sits in the same order the formula is written, so the page reads like the equation.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: denaturation time of 30 s, annealing time of 30 s, extension time of 45 s, cycles of 35, ramp time between steps of 4 s, starting copies of 1,000, amplification efficiency of 95%.

Substituting them into the formula gives time per cycle of 117 s, total run time of 68.25 min, fold amplification of 14,164,831,011 x, copies at the end of 14,164,831,011,411.

Those numbers come from the same solver the page runs in your browser, not from an illustration, so typing different inputs moves the answer exactly as the arithmetic says.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
The number on its own is not a judgement. These are the bands most often used when the result is quoted in a paper, a report or a label:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
90 – 100%Efficientclean primers, good template quality
80 – 90%Workablesome loss per cycle; enough product in 35 cycles
below 80%Poorinhibitors, primer dimers or wrong annealing temperature

  • Ramp time is not small: a three-step protocol ramps six times per cycle, and on a slow block that can add half a minute to every cycle.

  • Two-step protocols drop the separate extension step because the polymerase works at the annealing temperature, which is why fast protocols are so much shorter.

  • Efficiency above 100% in real data almost always means the baseline was set badly, not that the reaction invented copies.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
These are the errors that account for almost every wrong answer people bring to this calculator:

  • Forgetting the initial hot start and the final extension when quoting a run time.
  • Cutting extension time below about 30 s per kilobase for a long product.
  • Adding cycles instead of fixing a low efficiency — beyond about 40 cycles the plateau gives artefacts, not more product.

faq.q: How long does a 35-cycle PCR take?
faq.a: With 30 s denaturation, 30 s annealing, 45 s extension and 4 s ramps, about 70 minutes.
At 95% efficiency the target is multiplied by roughly 1.95³⁰ ≈ 5 × 10⁸.

faq.q: What does the PCR Cycle actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns time per cycle, total run time, fold amplification and copies at the end. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
